summary: This informational document illustrates use cases for Segment Routing in IPv6-only networks. Segment Routing steers packets through an ordered list of instructions using the source routing approach. The examples show how it can be applied in an IPv6 environment.

plainLanguage.summary: A trip can be planned as a list of stops. This gives examples of using such stop-by-stop plans for packets on the newer internet addressing system.

subtitle: Practical applications of source routing in IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: Traditional routing forwards packets along the optimal path determined by routing protocols, with no way for the source to control or influence the path through the network.
tldr.mechanism: Segment Routing (SPRING) for IPv6 allows a source (or ingress node) to embed a list of instructions, called segments, directly in the packet header. Each segment identifies a node or function to visit, and intermediate routers process them in order.
tldr.outcome: Operators gain fine-grained control over traffic flow without needing per-flow state in the network. This document illustrates five deployment scenarios where this is valuable.

facts.label: Core concept

facts.value: Instructions that identify nodes or functions to visit in order

facts.value: No per-flow state required in intermediate routers

today: RFC 8354 is an Informational document describing use cases and has not been obsoleted. It remains the reference for practical applications of IPv6 segment routing.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Source Packet Routing in Networking (SPRING) architecture, described in RFC 7855, leverages source routing: an ingress node includes a controlled set of instructions in a header at the start of the packet's journey. These instructions, called segments, are processed by intermediate routers as the packet traverses the network.

RFC 8354 illustrates practical use cases for Segment Routing in IPv6-only networks (often called SRv6). The scenarios show network operators how to apply source routing for traffic engineering, tenant isolation, load balancing, and other real-world requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, routers pick the best path automatically. With segment routing in IPv6, a sender can write "go through these routers in this order" in the packet, and routers follow that plan.

sections.title: Source Routing in Small Office Networks
sections.content:
Small Office, Home Office (SOHO) environments with IPv6 have multiple egress points connected to different ISPs, each with its own delegated IPv6 prefix. A customer edge router can classify traffic and steer it to the appropriate egress based on the packet's source address or associated prefix.

By encoding segment routes into packets at the customer edge router or at the end host itself, traffic can be directed to a specific egress to achieve regulatory compliance, service preferences, cost control (to avoid high data-cap links), or to segregate personal and work traffic in teleworking homes. Information in the SPRING header can also be used by applications and data centers at the destination to enable application-level steering and load balancing without relying on packet inspection.
sections.plainLanguage: A home has two internet connections. Segment routing lets you say "work traffic goes through this one, personal traffic through that one" without the router having to look inside each packet.

sections.title: Access Network Traffic Management
sections.content:
In cable access networks, an operator may want to map certain types of traffic to specific capacity pipes, such as DOCSIS service flows or QAM (Quadrature Amplitude Modulation) channels. In DOCSIS networks, different service flows represent different data links and can be differentiated for byte capping, regulatory compliance, or billing.

Instead of using implicit classification techniques (like Deep Packet Inspection), segment routing in the access device can map traffic based on information in the SPRING header. The source or edge router includes this mapping information in the packet, and the access device interprets it to route the packet to the correct downstream or upstream pipe without inspecting the packet contents.
sections.plainLanguage: An internet provider has different speed lanes. Segment routing lets the sender label their packets so they go into the right speed lane automatically, without the provider having to peek inside to classify them.

sections.title: Data Center and Content Delivery Networks
sections.content:
Data centers transitioning to IPv6-only infrastructure can use source routing (SRv6) to steer traffic across specific paths. The paths can include functions that intermediate nodes are requested to perform. This is useful for tenant isolation and multi-tenant scalability.

In Content Delivery Networks (CDNs), caches are organized in hierarchies with parent and sibling relationships. When a cache receives a request, it checks for content locally; if not found (cache miss), it forwards to the next cache in a list. By using segment routing to build these sequences, each cache can be uniquely identified by its IPv6 address, and the request path can traverse the cache hierarchy automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: A data center has many computers. Segment routing lets you say "send this customer's traffic through these machines in this order", so each customer gets isolated and correct service.

sections.title: Core Network Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
Large network operators building IPv6-only core infrastructure often need explicit path selection based on traffic type. If IPv6 customer prefixes are assigned by region or geography, the source address can identify the customer's location, and edge nodes can use segment routing to steer traffic through a specific (non-optimal) path for traffic engineering purposes.

Core operators may want to reserve high-bandwidth links for specific traffic types (like video), set up delay-sensitive paths for latency-critical applications, select specific exit points at multiple peering points, reach servers in facilities not reachable via optimal paths, or provision guaranteed disjoint paths (dual-plane networks) for diversity and resilience. Segment routing in IPv6 provides these capabilities without requiring per-flow state in intermediate nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: A big network has competing needs: some traffic is expensive, some is slow, some needs specific paths. Segment routing lets each sender say "my path goes through these nodes" so the network can balance everyone's needs.
